options.name: City
options.summary: The project sits in a dense, built-up neighbourhood. Land is scarce and costly. Transit and shops are right outside the door.
options.body:
A city project fits into streets that already exist. It is usually a compact building, sometimes squeezed onto a tight site or made by reusing an older one. Land is rare and tightly regulated, so the group spends a lot of time talking with the municipality and the neighbours.

Life outside the front door is already full. Transit and groceries are close by. Clinics and cafes are a short walk away. Many households can live without a car. Because so much is available nearby, the shared spaces inside can stay modest. They still matter, since they give a small group of neighbours a place to meet without leaving the building.

The Quebec guide says urban projects are often asked to open up to the street, since they sit so close to their neighbours. A ground floor with a shop or a public room helps the neighbourhood accept the project and ties the residents into local life.

The hard part is money and rules. Land costs the most here and zoning is strict. A small lot leaves little room for gardens or play space. Balconies and roofs often do that job. Shared cars and bikes are easier to justify when streets are crowded and parking is scarce. A group that picks the city gets convenience and connection, and pays for it in price and in patience with permits.
pros: Transit and shops are close by
The project ties into an existing neighbourhood
cons: Land is scarce and costs the most
Zoning and neighbours need constant dialogue
options.bestWhen: When the group wants to live without a car and close to work, and can afford the land and the permit process.

options.name: Suburb
options.summary: The project stands between city and countryside. There is more room for gardens and open space, but a car is often needed for daily errands.
options.body:
The suburb sits between city and country. Land costs less than downtown and there is more of it, so buildings can spread out and gardens can be bigger. Townhouses and low blocks are common, with generous outdoor space around them. The Quebec guide says this kind of site allows more open building shapes and bigger yards.

Shared spaces matter more here than in a city, because the shops are farther away. A common house or a garden becomes the place where neighbours meet. The guide says these spaces carry much of the project's social life and help the group share what it owns.

The weak point is getting around. Without planning, every errand needs a car, and a project can end up cut off from the area around it. Groups often respond with a shared car or a site near a station. The guide says the main challenge is balancing quality of life with access to the area.

The suburb suits groups who want a quieter pace and some space for children without moving far from jobs and schools. It is a middle path for many groups, with some of the room of the country and some of the reach of the city. Because shared yards and play areas are easier to fit here, families often find it a good match for daily life.
pros: More room for gardens and common spaces
Land costs less than in the city centre
cons: Daily errands often need a car
The project can feel cut off from the area

social.t: Shared spaces carry the social life

options.bestWhen: When the group wants space and quiet but still needs to reach jobs and schools within a short drive.

options.name: Countryside
options.summary: The project sits in a village or on open land. There is room for fields and nature, but services are far away and keeping the group full takes work.
options.body:
A rural project has the most land and the most freedom. Homes are usually grouped in a small cluster, like a little village, so that the fields stay open around them. The Quebec guide notes that this keeps some density, which helps neighbours meet. It also makes shared roads and utilities cheaper.

The group often lives close to farming and nature, and ties with local people tend to be strong. Shared spaces hold daily life together. They give the group room for meals and tools, and sometimes a small business. A new project can also help a village by bringing in families and letting older people stay in the place they know.

The cost is distance. Jobs and schools are far away, and so are clinics, a car is almost always needed, and the risk of isolation is real. Finding new members when someone leaves can take time, since fewer people are searching in a small area. The guide says the project must fit into the local economy to last. That means knowing the nearby farms and workplaces before moving in.

Local rules decide what can be built. In Quebec, regional county plans set the limits, so a group should check them before buying land. Water and power may also need to be brought in, which adds to the budget early on.
pros: Plenty of land and room to grow food
A project can bring new life to a village
cons: Services and schools are far away
Finding new members can be slow

governance.t: Few outside voices at the table

legal.t: Regional plans limit what is built

options.bestWhen: When the group wants land and a slower life, and is ready to deal with distance and car travel.

flags: Facts from the Quebec guide pp. 122-126, paraphrased. Examples rely on the setting tag in projects-data.js. 'Water, power and roads may also need to be added' is general knowledge, not from the guide.
